name: Superoxide dismutase
lead: Superoxide dismutase (SOD) is a family of metalloenzymes that convert the superoxide radical into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide and is regarded as a first line of antioxidant defense in most oxygen-using organisms. [2] The enzymatic activity was identified in 1969 by James McCord and Irwin Fridovich in a copper protein from red blood cells. [1]

In skincare and supplements SOD is used as an antioxidant ingredient, with the aim of limiting free-radical damage to skin from sun exposure and aging so that skin looks smoother and more even over time. It appears in antioxidant serums and creams and in oral products sold for skin, and the human enzyme itself is a well-studied part of the skin's own defense system.[2][12]

Registered human trials of SOD have mostly concerned radiation-related skin injury and oral supplements, including one oral SOD product for melasma. [3][4] No published trial of topical SOD for cosmetic anti-aging in healthy skin was found.

paras: SODs catalyse the dismutation of superoxide into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide, two less damaging species, at a rate close to the diffusion limit; the metal ion at the active site cycles between oxidation states during catalysis.[12] Copper-zinc forms are the most common in eukaryotes, manganese forms are found in mitochondria and many bacteria, and iron and nickel forms occur in bacteria and plant chloroplasts.[12]

Mammals have three main isoforms: SOD1 in the cytosol, SOD2 in mitochondria and SOD3 outside cells. [2] Variants of the SOD1 gene are associated with familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. [7] SOD sits within a wider literature on oxidative stress in conditions such as diabetes complications and cancer. [9][10]

Before its function was understood, the copper-zinc enzyme was known under names including erythrocuprein, hemocuprein and cytocuprein, and as the veterinary drug Orgotein. Wikipedia reports that Brewer described a protein in 1967 that was later recognised as SOD, and that Fridovich and McCord at Duke University discovered the enzymatic activity in 1968; their 1969 paper reported the enzymic function of erythrocuprein. [1][12]

Bovine liver SOD (orgotein) was used as an anti-inflammatory drug, with approval in several European countries for urinary tract inflammatory disease, and Wikipedia notes its use ended over prion-disease concerns.[12]

SOD is promoted as one ingredient in antioxidant serums and creams and in oral supplements sold for skin. Community discussion of it is sparse compared with ingredients such as vitamin C or retinoids.

Product makers have used animal, plant and bacterial sources, including bovine liver, marine phytoplankton, horseradish and cantaloupe.[12] Wikipedia states that ingested SOD is digested to amino acids before absorption, so unprotected SOD or SOD-rich foods are not shown to have physiological effects, and mentions that binding SOD to wheat proteins might improve activity in theory.[12] Formulation approaches for topical use therefore differ from those for small molecules, because the enzyme is a large protein.

Wikipedia describes tentative evidence, from studies lacking randomisation, blinding and placebo controls, that topical SOD may reduce free-radical damage and post-radiation fibrosis after breast cancer treatment, possibly by returning myofibroblasts to fibroblasts.[12] The SOD mimetic TEMPOL is in clinical trials for radioprotection and radiation dermatitis, and an oral SOD from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens has been tested for exercise-induced oxidative stress and in IVF patients.[12] Evidence on aging itself comes mainly from model organisms and SOD-knockout mice, where SOD loss shortens lifespan or increases oxidative damage.[12]
No cosmetic-specific safety data were found. Wikipedia notes that bovine-derived SOD drugs were withdrawn in several European countries over prion concerns.[12]

Registered human trials involving SOD include a completed trial of oral SOD (GliSODin) for melasma severity in 40 participants, a completed study of topical SOD for radiation-induced fibrosis in head and neck cancer patients (n=74), and a recruiting phase 2 trial (n=140) of an SOD skin spray for radiation dermatitis. [4][3][5] Other registrations involve diabetic neuropathy, male infertility and esophagitis during radiation. [6][8][11] A published randomised trial in diabetic neuropathy tested a combination product that included SOD together with palmitoylethanolamide, alpha-lipoic acid and vitamins, so the effect of SOD alone cannot be separated.[13] Results of the skin-related registrations are not summarised here, and none of these tested SOD for cosmetic anti-aging in healthy skin.

card.summary: An antioxidant enzyme added to anti-aging products; biologically central, but cosmetic evidence is essentially unstudied.
card.note: Registered trials concern radiation skin injury and oral supplements, not cosmetic anti-aging.

quick.overview:
Superoxide dismutase is a naturally occurring enzyme family that neutralizes the superoxide radical. It is added to some topical products and oral supplements marketed for antioxidant skin protection.

No published trial of topical SOD for cosmetic anti-aging was found; registered human trials concern mostly radiation skin injury and oral supplements.
quick.mechanism: SOD converts superoxide into oxygen and hydrogen peroxide. Humans have cytosolic (SOD1), mitochondrial (SOD2) and extracellular (SOD3) forms.
quick.risks: No cosmetic-specific safety data were found. Wikipedia notes that bovine-derived SOD drugs were withdrawn in several European countries over prion concerns.

chain: SOD (topical or oral) supplies or supports antioxidant enzyme activity
Superoxide and related reactive oxygen species from UV and metabolism are reduced
Less oxidative skin damage is proposed, supporting smoother, more even-looking skin
angle.text: SOD is added to antioxidant serums, creams and supplements so that skin has more enzyme-based protection against free-radical damage. Users and brands connect this to fewer visible signs of photoaging and pigmentation, mainly as a proposed mechanism.
